    On a monthly basis that’s almost next to nothing!

    There is a substantial drop-off in life insurance rates between a 20 year and a 30 year since underwriters do not have to worry as much about life expectancy.

    For many people, a 20-year policy gets them exactly where they want to be in life when the policy term runs out.

    Once again, you get a $200 drop in the annual premium by losing another 10 years on the term.

    If your life insurance agent isn’t giving you all these term options and is only focused on the death benefit, then you need a different agent.

    According to recent reports, for all you smokers out there – beware! The cost of your life insurance balloons as you’ll see here. If you’re considering kicking the habit, now is as good time as any.

    Some life insurance companies will give you a lower rate if you complete a recognized smoking cessation program, and go on without smoking for at least two years.

    It won’t help your immediate situation, but when you see the premium on smoker life insurance rates below, you might agree that it’s something to work toward!

    If you’ve made the decision that $1 million of life insurance is the right amount of coverage you need and you’re ready to purchase a policy, here are the steps you’ll need to follow.

    Sources indicate that 1. Determine How Much Coverage You Need: This is the first and most vital step in securing a million life insurance policies. You need to have a clear understanding of how much coverage you actually need.

    It has been revealed that 2. Choose the Right Type of Policy: There are whole life, term life, and Universal life policies available. Choose the one that best suits your needs.

    3. Shop Around: Don’t just go with the first life insurance organization you come across. It’s crucial to compare life insurance rates and coverage from a few different companies before making a decision.

    4. Consider Your Health: If you’re in good health, you’ll likely qualify for lower rates. However, if you have health issues, you may still be able to get coverage, but it will probably be more expensive.

    It has been revealed that 5. Consider Your Lifestyle: If you have a risky job or hobby, that could affect your rates.

    6. Get Quotes From Multiple Companies: This is the best way to compare rates and find the cheapest policy.

    7. Read the Fine Print: Make sure you understand all the terms and conditions of the policy before buying it.

    8. Buy Online: You can usually get cheaper rates by buying life insurance online.

    Industry observers note that 9. Pay Attention to Your Payment Schedule: Most life insurance policies require monthly or annual payments. Be sure you can afford the payments before buying a policy.

    In a recent development, 10. Review Your Policy Regularly: Life changes, and so do life insurance needs. Be sure to review your policy regularly to make sure it still meets your needs.

    Following these steps will help you get the best possible rate on a million-dollar life insurance policy.

    Recent findings suggest that make sure you understand all the terms and conditions before signing on the dotted line. Also, make sure to shop around and compare rates from multiple companies before buying a policy.

    According to recent reports, either way, you can get these larger amounts of coverage and still not break the bank. But get your policy now, while you’re still young and in good health.

    Industry observers note that the cost of a $1,000,000 life insurance policy will vary based on factors like your age, health, and lifestyle.     A target date fund is a mutual fund (or a similar pooled fund) built to be a single, all-in-one retirement investment. You pick the fund whose year is closest to when you initiative to retire, and the fund handles the rest. If you plan to retire around 2055, youâd choose a fund with 2055 in its name, like a Target Retirement 2055 or Target 2055 Index fund.

    It has been revealed that the fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and that mix shifts automatically as the target year gets closer. Early on, itâs mostly stocks for growth. As retirement approaches, it moves more money into bonds and cash to reduce swings in value.

    The appeal is obvious. You make one decision, contribute regularly and let the fund adjust itself. Thatâs why many 401(k) plans use a target date fund as the default investment for people who donât choose one.

    Recent findings suggest that most target date funds are a âfund of funds.â Instead of buying individual stocks and bonds, they hold other funds, usually a mix of U.S. stock, international stock and bond funds.

    For example, Vanguardâs fact sheet for its Target Retirement 2055 Fund dated September 30, 2026, shows it split among four main index funds: a U.S. total stock market fund (54.9%), a total international stock fund (36.6%), a U.S. bond fund (5.9%) and an international bond fund (2.6%).

    The glide path is the schedule that sets how the fundâs mix of stocks and bonds changes over time. Think of it as the fundâs long-term plan for gradually taking less risk.

    Schwabâs Target 2055 funds are a good example. Schwab says they start at 97% stocks and 3% bonds and cash, shift each year until they reach 44% stocks and 56% bonds and cash at the target date, then keep getting more conservative for 20 more years until they settle at 28% stocks.

    According to recent reports, the SEC explains that some funds use a âtoâ glide path, which stops changing at the target date, while others use a âthroughâ glide path, which keeps changing after it. âToâ funds generally get conservative sooner. Funds with the same target year can hold very different mixes, so check where a fund lands, not just its name.

    Most key, the glide path isnât built for you personally. Itâs a formula based on the target year. Your own risk tolerance, health, spending plans, pension or other income arenât part of it.

    According to recent reports, it depends on the fund. Index-based target date funds, like Vanguard Target Retirement and Schwab Target Index funds, hold index funds, so the investments inside are passive. The fund manufacturer still decides the glide path and the mix.

    Other target date funds use actively managed funds inside. Schwabâs regular Target Funds, for instance, combine active and passive strategies, including outside managers. Active versions usually cost more, as the next section demonstrates.

    Small differences add up. On a $100,000 balance, a 0.08% expense ratio costs about $80 a year, while 0.56% costs about $560 a year, every year, before any growth on the money youâd keep.     According to recent reports, the biggest selling point is that target date funds need almost no ongoing attention. You pick one fund, contribute regularly and leave it alone. If you have no interest in managing investments, that convenience is valuable.

    It has been revealed that because the fund holds U.S. stocks, international stocks and bonds, you get broad diversification in a single investment instead of betting on one company or sector.

    Recent findings suggest that over time, a portfolio drifts as different investments grow at different rates. A target date fund rebalances for you, which is one less thing to manage.

    Target date funds have real drawbacks, and for some investors theyâre enough to look elsewhere.

    Index-based target date funds can be very cheap, but actively managed versions can cost several times more, as the Schwab example demonstrates. In a 401(k), youâre limited to the version your blueprint offers.

    It has been revealed that the glide path is designed for a typical investor retiring in a given year. You might have a pension, a working spouse, rental income or a higher or lower risk tolerance than the fund assumes. None of that changes how the fund invests your money.

    You give up control over your mix. If youâd rather hold less international stock or fewer bonds, you canât change that while staying in the fund.

    Sources indicate that two funds with the same target year from different companies can have very different stock and bond mixes, holdings and fees. Without reading the details, itâs easy to end up in a fund that takes more or less risk than you expected.

    Sources indicate that the SEC points out that target date funds donât guarantee that youâll have enough retirement income, or any specific amount. They can lose money, including near or after the target date, because they still hold stocks.

    According to recent reports, an index fund simply tracks a market index, like the S&P 500. Thereâs no manager picking stocks, which is why costs are usually low. An index-based target date fund is really a bundle of index funds plus an automatic glide path, so the cost gap can be small.

    According to recent reports, the bigger difference is with actively managed target date funds. S&P Dow Jones Indicesâ SPIVA reports have repeatedly found that most actively managed U.S. stock funds trail their benchmark over long periods after fees. A target date fund full of active funds faces the same challenge, plus a higher expense ratio.

    A simple do-it-yourself alternative is the three-fund portfolio: a U.S. total stock market index fund, an international index fund and a bond index fund. You choose your own mix based on your age and risk tolerance and rebalance about once a year. It takes a little more effort, but you control the mix and can keep costs low.

    Target date funds arenât right for everyone, but they make sense in several situations:.

Investors who want more control often prefer a simple portfolio of index funds.

    Both kinds exist. Index-based target date funds, like Vanguard Target Retirement and Schwab Target Index funds, hold index funds, while others use actively managed funds inside. In either case, the fund tech giant decides the glide path that shifts the mix over time.

    Free Stores & Swap Shops – Check the Recycling Center & Library Before You Buy

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Before you buy household goods, clothes, or toys, look for a free store or swap shop near you, where people leave usable things for others to take at no cost.
    • It has been revealed that despite the name, many swap shops don’t require a swap.
    • Most sit at the town’s transfer station or recycling drop-off, where residents who haul their own trash leave household goods that still work, from kitchenware and tools to books and small furniture.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Before you buy household goods, clothes, or toys, look for a free store or swap shop near you, where people leave usable things for others to take at no cost. Try your town’s transfer station or recycling center, the library’s events calendar, and local churches. Bring only clean, working items, and take only what you’ll use.

    It has been revealed that despite the name, many swap shops don’t require a swap. A family short on money or settling into an empty apartment can leave with a lamp, a set of dishes, or a bag of toys without bringing a thing.

    Most sit at the town’s transfer station or recycling drop-off, where residents who haul their own trash leave household goods that still work, from kitchenware and tools to books and small furniture. Many are open only to residents, and some check for a transfer station sticker.

    It has been revealed that free stores work the same way, away from the transfer station. Churches and nonprofits run them, mostly for clothing and household basics, and some limit how much you take per visit. Public libraries hold swap days. Pop-up free markets, some called Really Really Free Markets, run once a month, often in a park. A toy swap or a book swap sticks to one kind of thing.

    Call 211 or search 211.org for free stores near you, and check the library’s events calendar for swap days. If you’ve just moved, get your transfer station sticker before your first visit. Bring what your household has outgrown, too. Parents who drop off kids’ clothes at a swap may leave with the next size up.

    Then follow the posted rules, which usually include these:.

    If your town has no swap shop, ask its public works department or recycling committee to add one at the transfer station. Massachusetts’ environmental agency even offers towns grants for one. Until then, host a clothing swap with friends, and ask your Buy Nothing group for the specific things you need.

    Search your town’s website for “swap shop” or “swap shed” before your next shopping trip, since the swap shop’s page lists the hours, the rules, and whether you need a sticker.

    The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

    Breaking: Business Equipment Without a Cash Crunch – Lease, Buy Used, or Repair

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Paying cash for upcoming equipment can leave your business short for payroll and inventory.
    • Recent findings suggest that buying outright looks thrifty, and it usually costs less over an asset’s life than leasing, the U.S.
    • In a recent development, so each option comes down to two numbers, the cash it takes up front and its total cost over the years you’ll use it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Paying cash for upcoming equipment can leave your business short for payroll and inventory. Before you buy, get quotes on a lease, a used model with a dealer warranty, and a repair of what you have. Then compare each one’s total cost over the years you’ll use it, after taxes.

    Recent findings suggest that buying outright looks thrifty, and it usually costs less over an asset’s life than leasing, the U.S. Small Business Administration notes. But that saving builds over years, while the whole price leaves your account the day you buy.

    In a recent development, so each option comes down to two numbers, the cash it takes up front and its total cost over the years you’ll use it. With new equipment, lowering one raises the other. A lease takes little cash up front but usually costs more in total than paying cash, and so does an equipment loan, once you add interest and fees. Buying the same model used lowers both, as long as it has plenty of working years left.

    Recent findings suggest that at tax time, lease payments are deductible as rent, while Section 179 of the tax code lets you deduct a purchase’s full price the year you start using it, up to yearly limits. A lease you can buy out for a token sum, such as $1, generally counts as a purchase to the IRS, so have a tax pro run each option’s after-tax cost.

    In a recent development, lease what you’d trade for a newer model within a few years, like computers. Before you sign, check how the lease ends: the buyout price, who pays to ship the equipment back, and how much notice stops it from renewing on its own.

    Buy used from a dealer that inspects or refurbishes the equipment and puts a warranty in writing. A restaurant that pays $9,000 for a two-year-old, dealer-certified range, when the same model costs $22,000 upcoming, keeps $13,000 as a cushion for its first slow season.

    Repair what you have when the repair costs less per year of use than a replacement. Say a $1,500 repair keeps an old range going three more years, and a $9,000 used one would last 10 years. The repair costs $500 a year, the replacement $900.

    Then pick the lowest total among the options that leave enough cash to cover your slowest month’s payroll, rent, and supplier bills.

    The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, if your health insurance premium jumped again this year, youâre not alone in looking for something cheaper.     Below I compare health sharing and traditional health insurance on cost, coverage, legal protection and risk, and explain who each one fits. I checked the 2027 Open Enrollment dates, premium trends and each programâs own rules in November 2026.

    Health sharing looks usually cost less each month than unsubsidized health insurance, but they arenât insurance: members share bills voluntarily, and nothing guarantees your bills get paid. Traditional insurance must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one and include benefits like maternity and mental health care, and subsidies can lower its price.     Sources indicate that costs are as of November 25, 2026. A health shareâs monthly price depends on your age, household and the amount you pay before sharing starts, so compare a quote with your own marketplace or employer price.

Michiganâs insurance regulator adds that they arenât classified as insurance because they donât take on risk and have no legal duty to pay membersâ costs.

    It has been revealed that most programs are Christian ministries with a statement of faith and lifestyle rules, such as no tobacco use. A few, like Zion HealthShare and Sedera, donât require a statement of faith.

    Recent findings suggest that example: Zion HealthShare is a nonprofit medical cost sharing community thatâs open to all faiths and has no provider network. Its Direct membership for individuals and families starts at $114 a month. Zion claims it is not insurance, and it canât accept members in Washington state. Read our Zion HealthShare review for its full rules.

    Traditional health insurance is a regulated contract: an ACA marketplace plan, an employer plan or another major medical policy. Under the Affordable Care Act, these looks must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one, and include the ACAâs essential health benefits, such as preventive care, maternity care, mental health care and prescription drugs. Healthinsurance.org explains the differences in detail.

    If you buy your own coverage, you use HealthCare.gov or your stateâs marketplace. Depending on your income, a premium tax credit can lower your monthly cost, and some lower-income enrollees also get help with deductibles and copays.

    Another option for the self-employed: Solo Health is a self-funded major medical health plan for people with their own business (you need an EIN). It uses a nationwide PPO network and a regulated captive insurance arrangement, and it claims it isnât a health share. You answer a health questionnaire to qualify. Read our Solo Health review for details.

    Insurance has gotten more expensive. KFFâs 2026 employer survey found that family coverage through work now averages $28,303 a year, with workers paying $7,471 of that on average. On the marketplace, the extra premium subsidies that started during the pandemic expired after 2025, and KFF reports that the average benchmark silver premium rose 26% for 2026 and is up another 13% for 2027. People earning more than 400% of the federal poverty level no longer get any premium tax credit and pay full price.

    According to recent reports, thatâs where health sharing looks appealing. Zionâs Direct membership starts at $114 a month, and Christian Healthcare Ministriesâ Bronze level is $115 per unit. Other programs, like Samaritan Ministries, list their own ranges.

    But the gap exists because health sharing programs donât have to guarantee anything. Insurance isnât friction-free either: HealthCare.gov insurers denied about 19% of in-network claims in 2024, according to KFF, and fewer than 1% of those denials were appealed. Still, an insurerâs denial comes with legal appeal rights and a state regulator you can complain to. A health shareâs review process follows its own guidelines, with no legal backstop if a bill isnât shared.

    Itâs a weaker fit if you have a chronic condition, are planning a pregnancy soon, need regular mental health care, qualify for a substantial subsidy, or simply want the certainty of a contract. For those households, the monthly savings usually arenât worth the risk of a large bill that isnât shared.

    Industry observers note that people often compare health sharing with direct primary care (DPC), but they do different jobs. DPC is a monthly membership you pay a doctorâs practice directly for primary care, such as office visits and basic labs. It doesnât cover hospital stays, surgery or emergencies.

    Outside Open Enrollment, you can only buy a marketplace plan if you have a qualifying life event, such as losing other coverage, moving, getting married or having a baby. Leaving a health share on its own usually doesnât count. So if you join a health share and then get a serious diagnosis, you may not be able to get insurance until the next Open Enrollment. KFFâs guide to 2027 Open Enrollment covers the other changes this year.

At the high end — peak travel season, last-minute pricing, transatlantic demand — that same seat hits $8,000 in cash, which means your LifeMiles are delivering **12.7 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1–2 CPP a baseline for points value. You're achieving 6 to 12 times that baseline. The reason this feels like a genuine inefficiency rather than just a deal: Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards on a **fixed award chart** that doesn't fluctuate with cash fare demand. When airlines raise transatlantic business class fares during summer holidays or major events, your points cost stays exactly the same. The gap between what the market charges and what LifeMiles charges simply grows wider. And then there's the no-fuel-surcharge policy — the detail that separates LifeMiles from competitors like British Airways Avios, which can pile $600+ in carrier surcharges onto a single redemption. With LifeMiles, you pay government taxes only, typically $50–$150 for a transatlantic itinerary. That's it. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption represents exactly the kind of asymmetric value that underpins a great travel rewards strategy: use points where cash prices are highest, eliminate fees wherever possible, and fly a product you'd never justify paying full price for — because you didn't have to.

Like all alliance programs, LifeMiles can sell award seats on partner airlines. The pricing is set by Avianca's own award chart, not by Lufthansa's chart or United's chart.

United MileagePlus charges 70,000–88,000 miles for the same seat. Avianca LifeMiles charges 63,000 miles with zero carrier surcharges. Same seat. Same plane. Wildly different cost.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, if you work 900 or more hours a school year as a preschool or K-12 teacher, aide, counselor, or principal, you can deduct up to $350 of classroom costs you paid yourself, even if you take the standard deduction. Keep the receipts for books, supplies, and training, and claim the deduction on Schedule 1 of your federal return.

    Every dollar of it comes off the income you’re taxed on, so in the 22% tax bracket, each $100 you deduct cuts your federal tax by $22. Starting with 2026 expenses, a second deduction can cover what you spend above the cap.

    According to recent reports, the IRS’s list of qualifying costs covers books, supplies, computers and software, other equipment and materials you use in class, and professional development courses related to your subject or your students. In health and gym classes, supplies count only if they’re athletic. Leave out anything your school, a grant, or another source paid you back for.

    A law signed in September 2026 extends the deduction to preschool and child care educators who meet the same 900-hour test, starting with 2026 expenses. Married educators filing jointly can each deduct up to $350.

    It has been revealed that the second deduction goes on Schedule A, the form where you itemize, or list your deductions instead of taking the standard deduction. The tax code sets no dollar limit on it, extends it to school coaches and athletic administrators, and covers nonathletic supplies for health and gym classes. It pays off only when your itemized deductions, such as mortgage interest and state and local taxes, add up to more than your standard deduction.

    A third-grade teacher who itemizes and spends $450 on books and supplies deducts $350 on Schedule 1 and the other $100 on Schedule A.

    Sources indicate that keep every receipt in one folder, paper or photos, with a note on what each item was for. The IRS generally has three years after you file to charge you more tax, so keep the folder at least that long.

    Recent findings suggest that are you trying to win the Mega Millions, but your numbers never seem to come up? It may be time to look for better ways to make money. Fortunately, you can earn extra cash without going and getting a “real job.”.

    Sources indicate that what are the best ways to avoid sitting in a cubicle all day? Some money-making strategies require an upfront investment, while others let you earn money in your free time with the help of apps.

    Read on to learn the best ways to earn cash without a regular 9-5 job, plus tips on how almost anyone can get started.

    One of the easiest ways to earn money is by signing up to participate in market research studies. You won’t make much, a few dollars here and there, but you can create a free account and get started within minutes.

    You’ll be paid in PayPal cash or gift cards for sharing your opinion and completing other tasks online.

    E-Poll Market Research is one of the top companies to consider for this type of work. They make it easy to create an account and answer survey questions.

    However, there are plenty of other options to consider, including:.

    While market research gigs won’t make you rich, it’s something you can do during your spare time.

    Recent findings suggest that if you have a book idea, turning your story into an eBook can help you earn passive income without a regular job. Kindle Direct Publishing can even help you format your book for Kindle, at which point you can market and sell your book to millions of potential readers who shop on Amazon.com.

    How much can you earn writing eBooks? That depends on how many books you write, how much you sell them for, and how successful you are at marketing your book. Selling 20 books per month with a profit of $7 per book would net you $140 per month and $1,680 per year.

    Meanwhile, selling 100 books per month at $7 per book would net you $700 per month and $8,400 per year. Need a little inspiration? Here’s an article that highlights you how to make your first $1,000 selling eBooks.

    In a recent development, you can earn a lot of money by starting a blog or niche website and monetizing it. I should know. I started Good Financial Cents more than a decade ago, and have earned millions of dollars through the monetization of this site since its earliest days.

    It has been revealed that how do you make money blogging? Earning real income with a website isn’t as easy as it looks, but there are plenty of monetization strategies you can try.

    Here are the most common ways blogs make money:.

    If you’re curious about what it takes to earn money blogging, consider signing up for my Make 1K Challenge. It’s free and can help you earn your first $1,000 online with some of the blog monetization strategies I’ve already mentioned.

    Recent findings suggest that you could argue that freelance work is like a regular job, but working at home and on your terms is much different from traditional employment. The fact is, most freelancers are fully remote – they can work from anywhere in the world with a laptop and an internet connection.

    Recent findings suggest that plus, they can hire and fire clients based on their personal needs and preferences, and their income potential is unlimited. According to ZipRecruiter, freelancers in the U.S. average $63.53 per hour.

    Of course, you’ll need a marketable skill to find paid work as a freelancer. This could be freelance writing, design skills, marketing expertise, or something else.

    You can use several websites to market your skills as a freelancer, including:.

    HealthyWage makes it possible to earn money while you lose weight. You won’t earn a ton of cash through the app, but you can earn a few dollars and use it to supplement other income you have.

    In a recent development, the more weight you lose, the more money you can make. For example, the HealthyWage website claims some of their clients who lost more than 100 pounds managed to earn anywhere from $1,400 to $3,000.

    However, the HW weight loss calculator highlights potential earnings of $578 to $828 for people who only have 15 pounds to lose.

    Industry observers note that if you have a car you rarely use and want to earn some side income, you can consider renting it out with Turo, a ride-sharing platform that connects car owners with people who need a short-term rental. You can set your price, although you’ll have more success if you price your car competitively.

    In a recent development, nicer vehicles in high-demand areas can easily fetch rates that surpass $100 per day through this platform. Turo notes that in-demand cars rented out regularly can bring in anywhere from $10,000 to $20,000 per year in net profit.

    Recent findings suggest that plus, almost anyone can rent out their car provided it meets the guidelines of the Turo platform. Your car must be 12 years old or newer with less than 130,000 miles. It must be worth less than $200,000 (no Lambo’s), and you must also meet Turo’s auto insurance requirements.

    It has been revealed that do you have a spare bedroom in your home that you never use? Maybe you have a basement or garage apartment you could fix up and begin renting for a profit?

    In a recent development, either way, Airbnb lets you rent out rooms and other spaces in your home on any dates you prefer. You must let renters know they’re renting a room in a home vs. an entire apartment or house and provide as much additional detail as possible.

    According to recent reports, the amount you can earn will depend on where you live and the type of accommodation you can offer. However, expensive cities like Chicago, New York, and San Francisco have plenty of rooms for rent that go for well over $100 per night.

    You may not have an entire room you can rent, but even if you have some storage space, Neighbor.com allows you to rent it out to others in need.

    Common spaces rented through this platform include.

    In a recent development, the Neighbor.com platform makes it easy to advertise your unused space so that people nearby can inquire if they’re interested. Also, note that the platform offers insurance that can protect you if some of your client’s items are damaged or stolen while in your care.

    Recent findings suggest that how much can you make renting out extra space? It depends on how much space you have to rent and where it’s located. However, Neighbor.com shows a range of rental space options that cost anywhere from $20 to $100+ per month.

    According to recent reports, investing in dividend stocks is one of the best ways to earn money without a regular job. Many early retirees find a way to live and pay bills based solely on the dividends they receive from various stocks.

    In a recent development, but what exactly is a dividend stock? For the most part, they are regular stocks but with a track record of sharing their profits with investors through dividends.

    Dividends can also be earned in exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds, and they can be significant once you build up a large portfolio.

    Since dividends are paid by profitable companies, they tend to be seen as less risky for investors. If you’re curious about what it takes to get started with this strategy, this post explains how to invest in dividend stocks.

    Housesitting is an option if you’re somewhat mobile and can move from place to place. Generally, you can find house-sitting gigs through word of mouth, referrals, or online portals like Craigslist.org or Facebook Marketplace.

    In a recent development, that said, not all house-sitting gigs are paid. Some offer the potential for exotic travel instead and free lodging for a week to several months.

    It has been revealed that either way, a website called TrustedHousesitters is the best place to find house-sitting gigs. Some jobs posted are for house-sitting only, while others require house sitters to provide basic care for pets or plants.

    If you have serious wanderlust and want to travel far and wide, this platform can help make it happen. Many gigs posted online are in countries like Australia, Ireland, France, and Switzerland.

    If you love animals and want to earn money taking care of them, several platforms can help turn your dream into a reality.

    For example, Rover.com lets you provide basic care for dogs or cats in your home, or you can pick up dog walking gigs. Another mobile app, called Wag!, lets you do more of the same.

    You can set your rates for all types of work through these platforms, and your availability. While earnings vary by location and job, most people watch dogs and cats for anywhere from $40 to $100 per night.

    Real estate investing may seem like a pipe dream if you hope to earn income without a job but hear me out. There are many ways to earn income through real estate without owning physical property or dealing with the hassles of being a landlord.

    You can invest in real estate investment trusts (REITs) that let you build wealth over time. You can also use a platform called Fundrise to invest in real estate with a minimum investment of $10.

    Fundrise lets you purchase eREITs, large investment funds that acquire, own, or operate multi-residential and commercial properties. The income you earn is entirely passive since it handles the work of finding income-producing properties and managing them.

    While returns are never guaranteed, Fundrise investors have achieved very solid returns. Investors who use the platform earned an average return of 7.31% in 2020, followed by 22.99% in 2021, 1.50% in 2022 and -7.45% in 2023 (their first down year).

    You can earn income on your spare change by investing it using Acorns. The roundup savings app syncs to your debit or credit card rounds up every purchase you make to the nearest dollar, and invests the difference. Once it’s set up, there’s no work on your part.

    Recent findings suggest that most of the money is invested in ETFs and managed by the world’s top investment firms like Vanguard and BlackRock. While this app makes it easy to invest small amounts of money, it’s not free to use. Personal plans start at $3 per month, while a family plan costs just $5.

    If you’re looking for some paid gigs that are relatively easy, consider setting up a profile on TaskRabbit, an online platform that lets you get paid for completing various tasks, such as:.

    Projects typically pay between $30 and $100, although some pay significantly more than that. TaskRabbit also lets you pick and choose the jobs you want to take on based on your availability so that you can work entirely on your schedule.

    If you love taking photographs and have a knack for getting professional-looking images, you can use your skills and expertise to sell photos online.

    Websites like Depositphotos and iStockPhoto pay photographers to supply them with stock photos they can sell to writers, publications, and various online platforms.

    In a recent development, the best part about this side hustle is that you can get started with the equipment you already have. While you can use a professional camera if you want to, many smartphones take professional-quality photos.

    Recent findings suggest that earning a bank bonus is another way to earn money without a regular job, but you’ll need an upfront investment to get started. Most bonus offers require you to deposit a specific amount of money and keep it in your account for up to 12 months.

    You may also be required to set up direct deposit to earn a bank bonus, and other terms and conditions may apply.

    Recent findings suggest that where can you find the best bank bonuses? While bonus offers constantly change, you can start by checking with banks like Chase, HSBC, Radius Bank, and Wells Fargo.

    Flipping furniture requires some upfront legwork and potentially even some artistic talent, but you can earn a solid income with this strategy if you know what you’re doing.

    Essentially, this side hustle requires you to shop at thrift stores, garage sales, and online platforms to find furniture that will ultimately sell for more than you paid.

    From there, you can sell the furniture as-is or clean it up and paint it with the goal of fetching an even higher price.

    You can make money driving for Uber or Lyft on your own time, picking and choosing the days and hours you want to work.

    Not only is rideshare work one of the most flexible side hustles, but you can earn $20 per hour and more with tips.

    If you are low on free time but still want to make money without a job, consider selling stuff you don’t need. An array of online platforms makes it a breeze, although some platforms work better for selling.

    For example, you can use Poshmark to earn money selling used clothing and accessories, while used electronics tend to sell best on platforms like eBay.com, Decluttr, BuyBackWorld, and Gazelle.

    If you have home decor, furniture, or workout equipment to sell, you’ll almost always do better unloading those items locally on Facebook Marketplace.

    Recent findings suggest that starting a YouTube channel is another way to earn money without a job, but that doesn’t mean it’s not work. The fact is, that creating quality videos and building an audience takes a lot of creativity and time. Plus, not everyone who tries to build a YouTube channel will succeed.

    Sources indicate that that said, you can earn income without a regular job. I know because I have done it with my YouTube channel, Wealth Hacker.

    How much you can earn on YouTube varies quite a bit, but it’s possible to earn thousands of dollars per month. If you’re curious about monetizing videos, my in-depth guide will show you how to make money on YouTube.

    In a recent development, donating plasma is a unique way to earn money without a job, although it’s not very glamorous. DonatingPlasma.org makes it easy to find plasma donation centers in your area, and you can earn as much as $100 for your first donation.

    That remarked, subsequent plasma donations typically earn closer to $50. You’ll also be limited by the number of times you can donate plasma within a month. However, it’s possible to use this side gig to earn an extra $500 per month, which you can use to supplement your primary income.

    If you are willing to complete various tasks that help regular workers do their jobs, consider becoming a crowd worker. This gig will have you finishing up to-do lists of jobs that don’t require specific technical skills.

    For example, you may get paid to proofread documents, label images, update a resume, complete a form, or complete a data entry assignment.

    Several platforms help you find crowd-working gigs, but the best ones include Microworkers and Clickworker.

    If you want to do something simple that will get you moving, consider delivering groceries using apps like Instacart or Shipt. You get paid hourly, plus tips and all you have to do is head to the store, purchase groceries according to a list, and deliver them to people in your neighborhood.

    The gig is extremely flexible, similar to driving for Uber or Lyft.

    Another non-job gig lets you get paid to deliver packages for Amazon.com. You can do this through a platform called Amazon Flex, which promises its drivers anywhere from $18 to $25 per hour.

    Recent findings suggest that unlike a regular Amazon job, Flex lets you pick the day and the hours you want to work. To get started, you need to create a free account, get approved, and start reserving blocks of time you want to deliver packages.

    Finally, you can earn money by selling unwanted or unused gift cards in your possession. This hustle is made easy thanks to platforms like GiftDeals.com and CardCash.com.

    Recent findings suggest that you won’t get the total value of your gift cards, but you should get 90% or more of the gift card balance for each card you sell. While selling gift cards for less than their total value may not seem ideal, it’s better than not using them and getting nothing in return.

    Finally, you can earn small amounts of money by signing up with the best online survey sites. Not only is this side hustle as easy as it gets, but you can participate and get paid during your spare time and even on your phone.

    Other online survey sites to check out include the following:.

    It has been revealed that there you have it, 26 ways to make money without a job. While many of the jobs on our list won’t replace your 9-5, they can be a great way to increase your income so you can pay off debt or break the cycle of living paycheck to paycheck.

    Kids’ Clothes on Clearance – Buy Next Year’s Size, Not This Year’s

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Latest kids’ clothes cost the least at end-of-season clearance, but your child’s current size likely won’t fit when that season comes back.
    • The biggest markdowns come twice a year.
    • From age 2 until adolescence, children usually grow about 2½ inches a year, according to Nemours KidsHealth.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Latest kids’ clothes cost the least at end-of-season clearance, but your child’s current size likely won’t fit when that season comes back. Shop for next year instead, usually one size up, and bring a list of what each child still needs so the markdowns fill real gaps.

    The biggest markdowns come twice a year. Stores clear winter coats and snow pants after the holidays, and swimsuits and shorts in July, to make room for the next season’s stock.

    You can predict next year’s size. From age 2 until adolescence, children usually grow about 2½ inches a year, according to Nemours KidsHealth. That’s about one size on a typical kids’ size chart.

    Sources indicate that say your child wears a size 4 this winter, and a size 5 coat and snow pants cost $35 on clearance in January or $90 at full price next October. Buying in January saves $55 on clothes your child will need either way.

    To find next year’s size, measure your child’s height, add 2½ inches, and look up that height on the brand’s own size chart, since sizes vary by brand. Babies grow faster, about 10 inches on average in their first year, so buy them the size labeled for the age they’ll be a year from now. Stretchy knits and adjustable waistbands still fit when your guess is a little off.

    Bring a list to the sale. Count what each child already has in next year’s size, including clothes with room to grow, hand-me-downs, and secondhand finds. Then write down only the gaps, such as a coat and two pairs of pants.

    According to recent reports, leave shoes and boots off the list and buy them when they’re needed. The American Podiatric Medical Association notes that a child’s shoe size may change every few months, and it advises measuring the feet before buying shoes.

    Store each purchase in a bin labeled with the size and season, and open that bin before you shop when the season comes back.

    • In a recent development, the Agriculture Department publishes the income limits each year by household size, at 185% of the federal poverty line for reduced-price meals and 130% for free ones.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Before you pay for or pack another school lunch, find out whether your kids can get free or reduced-price meals. Your school or state may already feed every student free, and kids in families on SNAP food benefits get free meals automatically. Otherwise, fill out the school’s meal application each school year, or whenever your income drops.

    A family of four earning $55,000 a year qualifies for reduced-price meals this school year, and a reduced-price lunch costs 40 cents at most. With two kids buying lunch every day of a 180-day school year, that family saves $936 by paying 40 cents instead of $3.00, the typical elementary lunch price in a School Nutrition Association survey.

    In a recent development, the Agriculture Department publishes the income limits each year by household size, at 185% of the federal poverty line for reduced-price meals and 130% for free ones. Kids whose families get SNAP food benefits or TANF cash assistance qualify for free meals regardless of income, as do children in foster care, in Head Start, or experiencing homelessness.

    According to recent reports, nine states make school meals free for all public school students: California, Colorado, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Newly introduced Mexico, New York, and Vermont. Elsewhere, many schools serve every student free breakfast and lunch, with no applications, under the federal Community Eligibility Provision.

    In a recent development, start by asking your kids’ school whether meals are free for everyone there this year. If they aren’t, look for a letter saying your kids were approved through SNAP or another benefit, which schools must send when no application is needed.

    Otherwise, fill out the free and reduced-price meal application, one form for all your kids in the district. Turn it in any time during the school year, including right after a job loss or pay cut. File a fresh one every school year, since an approval expires no later than 30 school days into the next. Federal rules bar schools from posting or announcing approved kids’ names, or singling them out in the lunch line.

    If you pay full price, add up what your packed lunches cost before assuming they’re cheaper. Deloitte’s 2026 school lunch index put its cheapest packed lunch, built around a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, at $4.89, against $3.00 for a typical elementary school lunch.

    #125423. How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

    📅 13 Jun 2025 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2449 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

    📅 13 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2449 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well.
    • And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.
    • As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well. Back in February 2025, the market put the perfect cap on a multi year climb before stepping onto the wild roller coaster we’re presently riding. Since then it has seen some of the steepest drops and recoveries in history, losing a full 20% of its value at the bottom while somehow managing to end up right back near the peak as I’m writing this.

    And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.

    As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.

    Industry observers note that as I write this, we still don’t know the outcome of the worldwide tariff and trade battle that our unpredictable government has unleashed upon the world. But we’re already seeing the results: businesses are bracing for massive changes, currencies and interest rates are reacting, and regular investors like you and me are wondering what the future holds for our early retirement funds. Surveying my own group of friends, the reactions span the whole range of emotions from “this is a giant Nothingburger” to “we’re all totally screwed.”.

    In a recent development, so what’s the real answer? To get closer to that, we should start with the most basic question of:.

    A tariff is just a sales tax charged by our government on goods which are imported into the country. They are paid by whoever is doing the importing – meaning you if you order something like an e-bike directly from a tech giant in China, or by companies like Amazon, Walmart, or Apple which import products from other countries by the shipload.

    Sources indicate that but in the end, the tariffs aren’t paid by China or Amazon or Apple. They are paid by you, the end consumer, because if their cost of goods increases, a retailer is of course going to raise their prices to continue to make a profit.

    It has been revealed that tariffs also affect companies directly: if Home Depot wants to build a newly introduced store or Chevron needs a new oil rig, the tariffs on imported steel, copper, lumber and a million other components will raise the cost of these construction projects. And they raise the cost of housing, because most of the building materials in houses come from multiple countries as well.

    It has been revealed that on average, tariffs will result in higher prices for everything just like any other broad-based sales tax. And just like most other taxes, the overall effect is to slow the economy and reduce our spending power. On the positive side, all that tax money flows into the government’s pocket which could help fund the national budget and even reduce the deficit.

    Of course, every government needs at least some tax revenue to function, so it makes sense to use some mix of sales, income and corporate taxes to get there. The most crucial part is that the levels need to be as low as possible while still keeping the country running well, and as fair and predictable as possible, so that people and businesses have an incentive to work hard and the ability to blueprint far into the future.

    It has been revealed that and that’s where our current tariff regime gets it completely backwards. Donald Trump is throwing around random, extremely high tariff numbers as threats, then walking them back and changing them on an almost daily basis..

    Whoa, that Sounds Mostly Bad – Is There a Good Side of Tariffs?

    Recent findings suggest that sometimes, a country will use tariffs to protect their own domestic industries. For example, if you put a tax on imported Hondas, then General Motors cars will gain a competitive advantage – so GM will make more money. In this example, most consumers end up losing due to increased prices and decreased selection. But at least domestic auto manufacturers and their employees are happy.

    This can be strategic (for example we might want to slap a tax on imported fighter jets to make sure Boeing and Lockheed can remain in business, for national defense purposes.) Or it can be corrupt (a politician might receive funding from kingpins in the steel industry, and in return then push through tariffs on imported steel to protect the profits of US steelmakers.).

    And this isn’t just a Trump or Republican thing either – Joe Biden used tariffs during his terms in an attempt to please swing-state voters. One of the worst examples was a tax on imported solar panel components (which Trump has since raised even further, proving that Boneheadedness can be Bipartisan). These are sheets of cheap glass that literally pump the cheapest energy and easiest wealth into your country for 30 years as soon as you plug them in. Cheap energy lowers everyone’s cost of living while also boosting industry. There is no good reason to block such wealth from flowing across your borders.

    Can Tariffs Bring Us More Jobs?

    Industry observers note that let’s go back to that hypothetical tax on Hondas, and let’s say it’s a big one like $5000. At that level, many buyers will start heading over to the GM dealer next door to consider what he’s selling. Sure, the GM cars may not be as good, but for five grand some people are going to settle in order to save some money.

    Because of this, GM’s sales go up. So they hire more employees and build more factories. They might even develop some fresh models and new technologies in response to all that new demand. More people learn advanced skills and in the best case it becomes a virtuous circle.

    Industry observers note that but in exchange for this boom in the auto industry, everyone else has to pay more for slightly shittier cars and trucks. Higher vehicle prices means Amazon will have to spend more on their delivery fleet, so they will raise prices slightly on everything they sell. Somewhere a startup company or a medical breakthrough will be just a bit less likely to happen, because they are operating in an environment that is just a bit more expensive and a bit less efficient.

    Industry observers note that on top of that, with GM liberated from the hassle of competing with Honda, it will have less incentive to innovate and streamline itself. So its overall trajectory will be slower and less efficient even if its profits are higher.

    According to recent reports, this massive picture effect is why most economists agree that tariffs should be used very sparingly. They almost always cause unexpected damage, decrease overall employment and slow down an economy, but sometimes (like for food security or national defense) those costs are worth paying.

    So Why is Donald Trump Throwing Around Tariffs Like They Are The Best Thing Ever?

    This has been confusing to almost everyone. If you take him at his word, he appears to have a Bizarro Opposite Universe belief system about economics. Donald has claimed in speeches that the tariffs will somehow make us wealthier. He’s focusing on the first-order effects like GM hiring more workers, while completely ignoring the fact that everything else in the country gets less efficient in exchange.

    In a recent development, but when he announces larger tariffs, share prices go down, because everyone who actually runs or invests in US companies knows that of course they will make less money on average. When tariffs are paused or reduced, share prices go back up. Yet he keeps wielding the threats and we go back and forth.

    It seems to be obvious to everyone except Donald himself that Tariffs are just a national sales tax rather than some clever sneaky strategic weapon, which leads to various theories that okay, maybe he knows that too but is just pretending in order to gain some influence.

    The basic theory goes like this:.

    According to recent reports, so right now our entire economy is subject to the whims of a single person.. And as long as this is the case, we’re just the same as any other dictatorship – something our constitution was supposed to prevent with the whole “three independent branches of government” thing.

    But presidents have tried to break out of their constitutional cage and get more power many times in the past, and this is just the latest example. The real test will be if our system eventually manages to stop this abuse and put itself back in balance as it always has in the past. You can already see this fight beginning to play out in our court system, in this Economist article:.

    How Substantial are the Tariffs Right Now?

    According to recent reports, even without the 145% nonsense numbers that were thrown around a few months ago, they are still far higher than they have been in the last 75 years or more. While it would be hard to pin down the current numbers in a stationary blog post like this one, the key thing to remember is that our current US economy is built around very low tariffs and relatively free trade.

    Why haven’t I noticed Prices Going Up Yet?

    While the US economy is fueled by a constant stream of cargo ships, as a whole we function like the biggest cargo ship of all: we have a huge inventory and it takes a while to change directions.

    Recent findings suggest that so in normal times, we already have several months of inventory of most things in the country. And then when all this drama started, importers started placing even more orders to stockpile things in advance before the tariffs hit. And now that they are in place, we’re importing a lot less stuff.

    For now, we’re still using up the stockpiled inventory, but imports have dropped significantly so we’re promptly running out of cheap goods. If that happens, we will probably start seeing shortages and price increases throughout this summer or fall. For some things like plastic party trinkets, we can do just fine without. But if we lose access to core useful things like tools and machinery, the economic consequences will be much less fun.

    The Dark Side and the Bright Side.

    Sources indicate that the most vital phrase to remember in US politics and economics is the phrase “This too shall pass.” The only mystery right now is that we don’t know exactly how it will pass. So we could sketch out a few scenarios:.

    1) The current crazy-high tariffs really do stick around:.

    I personally think this is the less likely scenario because nobody really wants it. But just as a thought experiment, it might go something like this:.

    2) They do end up being just a negotiating tactic and we go back to mostly low tariffs.

    In other words, the best way to win the tariff game is not to play it.

    According to recent reports, just as much of US prosperity is built upon our huge population of 330 million people living in 50 states with open borders and no trade restrictions, all (friendly) countries of the world can benefit from the free exchange of goods, services and even people. We’re all human beings and if we treat each other with a collaborative respect, we all grow richer.

    Epilogue: Is it Almost Over Already?

    I started writing this article on April 2nd, when Donald declared his “Liberation Day” and the stock market reacted with the biggest drop since 1932. Some people panicked and locked in big losses despite decades of warnings from your favorite financial bloggers, like this unfortunate soul in the comments to a JL Collins post:.

    But as I watched over the next two months, we have bounced our way back up – with each drop in proposed tariffs triggering a corresponding increase in stock prices (a measure of investor enthusiasm of how bright our future looks).

    Recent findings suggest that right now, the US stock market is just about back to its all-time high. This doesn’t match with our current level of tariffs, which are still about seven times higher than they were before the circus opened. But it reveals that investors believe it’s all going to end with a truce and a resumption of free-ish international trade.

    Industry observers note that if they’re wrong, the roller coaster ride will still have some more fun in store for us. But as long as we eventually end our current experiment in “emergency” tariff dictatorship and get back to functioning as a democracy, things should be just fine in the long run. I’m still 100% invested myself, so that’s where I place my bet.

    The Biggest Lesson: Don’t Form Your Opinions Based on News Headlines.

    Decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us, with just a bit of sizzle and spice to pull in our attention. Unfortunately, nowadays the priorities have flipped where the primary goal is attention, and accuracy carries little or no weight. Even a totally inaccurate article makes money for the publisher.

    So while Democrats and Republicans like to do battle over which media sources are biased, in reality they’re all wrong: all click-funded commercial media is biased – sometimes politically but even more importantly biased towards generating outrage and fear, because those generate more money.

    There are two solutions to this:.

    1) Either ignore the media completely and focus on your own life, or.

    2) Become a subject matter expert on things you really care about, and then read the original sources whenever you want to learn about something.

    Recent findings suggest that I mostly practice option #1, but as a science and technology nerd I get into #2 in just the areas I find most interesting. And it’s amazing how the more deeply you understand a subject, the more you see just how wrong most media stories are about your area of expertise. Which means they’re probably pretty wrong about almost everything.

    Industry observers note that so as always, with this lesson learned it’s time to shut down that phone and laptop, exhale all our worries and get back outside with your real-life family and friends. See you in a few months!

    #125421. Earned Income Tax Credit – Check Every Year, Even If You Didn’t Qualify Before

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

    Earned Income Tax Credit – Check Every Year, Even If You Didn’t Qualify Before

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (497 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, if you work and earn a low or moderate income, check whether you can claim the earned income tax credit (EITC) every year before you file.
    • Industry observers note that about one in five workers who qualify for the EITC don’t claim it, by the IRS’s estimate.
    • Your earned income from work and your adjusted gross income (AGI), which counts your other income too, must both fall under the IRS’s income limit for your filing status and how many qualifying children you claim.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, if you work and earn a low or moderate income, check whether you can claim the earned income tax credit (EITC) every year before you file. A pay cut, a new baby, or a divorce can change the answer. The credit is refundable, so it pays you even if you owe no tax.

    Industry observers note that about one in five workers who qualify for the EITC don’t claim it, by the IRS’s estimate. The credit is worth up to $8,231 to a family with three or more children and up to $664 to a worker with none.

    Your earned income from work and your adjusted gross income (AGI), which counts your other income too, must both fall under the IRS’s income limit for your filing status and how many qualifying children you claim. The IRS adjusts the limits for inflation each year. You also need investment income under a yearly cap and a valid Social Security number for you, a spouse on a joint return, and each child you claim. Without a qualifying child, you or a joint-filing spouse must be 25 to 64 at year’s end.

    Take a single parent with two qualifying children and no income but her pay, which came to $28,000 in 2026. By our math from the IRS’s 2026 figures, her credit is about $6,450.

    Start with the IRS’s EITC Assistant, which says whether you qualify and estimates your credit. To claim it, file Form 1040, adding Schedule EIC if you claim a qualifying child. Even if your pay was too low to require a return, file anyway to collect it. Your 2026 return may also need the IRS’s upcoming Schedule 3-A, which asks whether you want your “federal public benefit,” the refunded part of your credits. Answer yes.

    IRS-certified volunteers at Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (VITA) sites, which mainly serve workers who meet the EITC’s income guidelines, prepare basic returns free. The IRS’s VITA Locator finds sites near you.

    In a recent development, by law, the IRS holds the entire refund on any return claiming the EITC until mid-February. The parent above, filing early online with direct deposit and no problems on her return, can expect hers by early March, under the IRS’s schedule.

    Use Form 1040-X to claim the credit on any earlier return you filed without it, within three years of that return’s due date.

    Filers who’d rather prepare their own return can compare the best free tax software.

    Having more than one type of debt is common, and that’s especially true once you graduate from college and start your first “real job.” You may have credit card debt, an auto loan, and a mortgage payment to make once you buy your first home. It’s also common to have other random debts to cover, including student loans.

    If you’re like many who took out loans during college, you will likely be paying them off after you graduate. In fact, 82% of students who borrowed loans expect to be making payments post-graduation, according to a recent College Ave Student Loans survey.

    That said, you’ll want to make sure you’re balancing debt repayment with your savings goals along the way.

    It has been revealed that you’ll also want to make sure you’re paying down debts in the optimal order, or in a way that will help you save the most money on interest as possible while aligning with your goals. Which debts should you pay off first? Here’s a rundown of how to get the best results:.

    It has been revealed that no matter which types of debt you have, credit card debt should be your first priority. Why? Because credit card debt is likely the most expensive debt you have by far.

    Federal Reserve data indicates the average credit card interest rate on accounts assessed interest came in at around 22% as of May 2023, yet your credit card could easily be charging higher rates than the average.

    To save as much money as possible, you should strive to pay as much as you can toward high-interest credit card bills each month. You can also pay down credit card debt faster with the help of a debt consolidation loan or a 0% APR balance transfer credit card.

    According to recent reports, other unsecured debts like personal loan debt should come next in the debt payoff pecking order. After all, unsecured debts tend to have higher interest rates than secured debts like auto loans. In fact, the Federal Reserve also reported that the average interest rate on a 24-month personal loan came in at 11.48% as of May 2023, compared to the average rate of 7.81% on a 60-month auto loan.

    Ideally, you’ll start paying more toward personal loan debt and other unsecured debts after all credit card debt is entirely paid off, although you should make at least the minimum payment on all your bills throughout the entire process.

    The next debt you’ll want to tackle is your student loans. I suggest focusing on these loans after other unsecured debts, since federal student loans (and many private student loans) come with low fixed interest rates and monthly payments that will not change over time. If you have federal student loans, you may even want to look into income-driven repayment prepares.

    If you’re hoping to pay down student loans faster or just want to save money on interest, you can also consider refinancing your student loans to get a shorter repayment timeline, a lower monthly payment, or both. Just remember that refinancing federal student loans can mean losing access to income-driven repayment prepares and federal protections like deferment and forbearance.

    Once you have paid off or substantially paid down all your other debts, you can focus your efforts on secured debts you have like mortgage loans and auto loans. These debts should be dealt with last since they are secured with collateral and tend to offer lower interest rates as a result. For example, you can consider paying more than the minimum on your mortgage, a car loan, or both until they’re paid off completely.

    Then again, you may want to pay off debts with extremely low interest rates as slowly as possible to free up more cash flow for living expenses and investments. If you took out a mortgage in January of 2021 when the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed rate home loan was as low as 2.65%, for example, it makes sense to make the minimum payment on that debt and invest your extra cash instead.

    Sources indicate that it’s important to make sure you balance debt repayment with other financial considerations. After all, focusing too much on debt repayment early in life can leave you behind when it comes to investing for retirement or saving up for a first home.

    While you’ll want to eliminate credit card debt and other high-interest debts as promptly as you can, even if you have to stop saving and investing for a while, you can pay down student loan debt and secured debts at a slower pace while saving and investing for the future along the way.

    Finally, make sure you have adequate emergency savings throughout your entire debt payoff journey, or that you begin saving for emergencies as soon as you can. Without a fully funded emergency fund, you can end up relying on credit cards and other loans to get by and ruin your debt payoff progress in the process.

    According to recent reports, how much should you save? While most experts recommend having an emergency fund that can cover three to six months of expenses, it’s okay to start small if you have to.

    Having more than one type of debt is how it works for most people, especially when you’re young and in the early stages of your career. When it comes to paying it off, however, you’ll want to make sure you have a concrete plan that can help you reduce interest charges and get where you want to be.

    Sources indicate that focusing on credit card debt and other unsecured debts first always makes sense, since these debts aren’t secured by an asset and tend to charge much higher interest rates. You can focus on student loans next, followed by other secured debts you have like a home loan or car loan.

    Recent findings suggest that in the meantime, make sure you have an adequate emergency fund and invest in it for retirement. After all, debt won’t last forever if you’re serious about repayment, and saving and investing early can help you benefit from compound interest and avoid using credit cards for surprise expenses. Creating a budget to track these factors is your best bet.

    If you need help creating one, or simply don’t know where to start, use this budget worksheet as your guide – you’ll reach financial freedom in no time.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
    • Business class hops across Europe for fewer points than most domestic economy awards.
    • Picture this: you've just crossed the Atlantic on a long-haul award, touched down at London Heathrow, and now you need to get to Rome for the real adventure to begin.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

    Business class hops across Europe for fewer points than most domestic economy awards.

    Picture this: you've just crossed the Atlantic on a long-haul award, touched down at London Heathrow, and now you need to get to Rome for the real adventure to begin. Most travelers at this point resign themselves to a cramped economy seat on a budget carrier, dragging luggage through a secondary terminal. But you? You're walking into the Virgin Atlantic clubhouse, sipping a Bloody Mary, and then settling into a proper business class seat for the 2.5-hour hop to Fiumicino. That's the magic of this redemption. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class seat on a short-haul European flight — London Heathrow to Rome, London to Athens, London to virtually any major European city — routinely retails for **$1,000 to $3,000 in cash**. Airlines know that business travelers on these routes are often on corporate accounts and will pay whatever it costs. The leisure traveler simply doesn't book business class on a two-hour flight because it feels absurd. And that's exactly the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community learns to exploit. Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club prices these short-haul European business class seats at a flat **17,500 miles one-way**. At the low end of that $1,000–$3,000 cash range, you're already extracting **5.7 cents per point** — well above what most programs deliver. At the high end, when those seats spike to $3,000 on peak travel dates, you're looking at a staggering **17.1 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1.5–2 cents per point a solid redemption. This one can deliver *ten times* that. What makes this feel particularly right for the FI mindset is the positioning angle. This isn't just a standalone splurge — it's the finishing move on a transatlantic trip you've already largely funded with points. You've landed in London. You need to get to your final European destination. Instead of paying $200 for a budget airline seat that charges extra for your carry-on, you drop 17,500 Virgin miles and arrive refreshed, fed, and ready. The opportunity cost of those miles is low; the experiential upgrade is enormous. This is what travel rewards done right looks like: not flying business class because you're wealthy, but because you understood the system better than the airlines expected you to.

    The core insight here is understanding how Virgin Atlantic prices its own metal versus partner awards — and then deliberately choosing the right one for the right job.

    It has been revealed that virgin Atlantic's Flying Club is famous in the points community for two things. First, its partner award sweet spots: ANA First Class for as low as 55,000–60,000 miles one-way, Delta One at competitive rates. These are the headline acts. But quietly sitting in the same award chart is a genuinely underappreciated gem — Virgin's own short-haul European business class, priced at a flat 17,500 miles regardless of the specific route within that distance band.

    Why does Virgin price it this way? Virgin Atlantic operates as a premium carrier and sets its award chart to reflect aspirational redemptions — the kind that make Flying Club membership feel worthwhile.     • Families with kids in elementary through high school planned to spend an average of $146.45 on school supplies in 2026, according to the National Retail Federation’s annual back-to-school survey.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Before you buy school supplies, gather last year’s leftovers, from backpacks and binders to calculators and pens, and cross everything that still works off the teacher’s list. Then buy only what’s still missing, and get the basics during July’s back-to-school sales, when folders, notebooks, and crayons can cost under a dollar each.

    Industry observers note that A leftover you reuse costs nothing this year, so it beats even those sale prices. And the priciest things a list asks for, like a backpack, a binder, or a calculator, usually outlast the school year.

    Families with kids in elementary through high school planned to spend an average of $146.45 on school supplies in 2026, according to the National Retail Federation’s annual back-to-school survey. Say two kids’ lists come to $120 at regular prices, and two backpacks and a calculator make up $60 of it. Reuse those three, buy the other $60 of supplies on July’s deals for about $40, and the year’s supplies cost $40 instead of $120. Three-quarters of that $80 saving comes from the backpacks and calculator you didn’t buy.

    Recent findings suggest that start with the house. Empty last year’s backpacks, desk drawers, and pencil boxes, test every marker and glue stick, check zippers and straps, and write down what still works.

    According to recent reports, then wait for the teacher’s list and buy only what it asks for, in plain versions rather than character-branded ones your child may outgrow by next year. If the list won’t arrive until the first week of school, buy pencils and notebooks in July and leave anything specific, like a binder size or a calculator model, until it does.

    According to recent reports, buy the basics in July, when office supply chains sell 2-pocket folders for 25 cents and boxes of crayons for 50 cents, often with a limit per customer. For a calculator or another item the list names by model, Staples and Office Depot will match another store’s lower price, though each excludes some sales. For supplies every child uses up, like pencils and glue sticks, a warehouse club’s bulk pack can cover all your kids. First compare its unit price, the price per item, with what each item costs on sale in July. Save the pricier items still on the list for your state’s sales tax holiday, if it has one.

    When school lets out, put whatever survived the year in one bin, and open it before you shop next summer.
