    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that several family chains let kids eat free one or two days a week, usually with one free kids’ meal for each paying adult entrée, and a couple let young kids eat free any day. Plan your family dinners out around those days, and confirm your location runs the deal before you go.

    In a recent development, at Luby’s, where a kids’ meal costs $6.49, two adults with two kids 10 or younger who eat there on a kids-eat-free day pay only for their own meals and save $12.98. Four such dinners a month save $51.92.

    In a recent development, most of these deals work the same way. Each paying adult entrée earns one free kids’ meal for a child at or under an age cutoff, usually 10 to 12. Several chains also count only meals eaten in the restaurant.

    That one-for-one ratio is the catch for bigger families. Two adults with three kids still pay for one kids’ meal, and some chains cap the free meals per table or per check instead of per adult.

    These eight chains run their deals on set days of the week, listed from Tuesday on.

    These two chains let young kids eat free every day of the week.

    In a recent development, some buffets also price kids’ meals by age. At the Pizza Ranch in Ames, Iowa, kids 1 to 12 pay $1.09 for each year of age, so a 6-year-old’s buffet costs $6.54.

    On days without a deal, ordering water and sharing plates keeps the kids’ share of the bill low, and restaurant apps and birthday clubs give out free meals of their own.

    Not every restaurant in a chain runs its deal. Red Robin, Smashburger, and Dickey’s limit theirs to participating locations, and Pizza Ranch’s age cutoffs and hours vary by location.

    Smashburger and Dickey’s won’t combine their deals with any other offer, and Red Robin won’t combine its deal with its rewards, so save a coupon or reward for another visit. Ask whether the free kids’ meal includes a drink.

    Pick the day that fits your week, then call the restaurant that day to confirm it’s running the deal and how many free kids’ meals your table gets.

    #125409. How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

    📅 07 Oct 2025 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2045 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

    How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

    📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon.
    • You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.
    • I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun fresh way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which stated something like,.

    “Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.

    I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

    “Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

    Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”.

    So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

    And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:.

    According to recent reports, okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

    But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

    So I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

    Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect.

    Industry observers note that one of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:.

    As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:.

    Sources indicate that but occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

    As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

    I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

    Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

    Sources indicate that I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

    Then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

    So Was This The Downfall of MMM?

    Industry observers note that during the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

    Recent findings suggest that but eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

    But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

    Industry observers note that admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

    Recent findings suggest that I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

    Sources indicate that then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

    This is What “Fuck You Money” is For!

    It has been revealed that it dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

    According to recent reports, it reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

    Experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning newly introduced things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

    Industry observers note that one interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:.

    So I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

    Thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

    Sources indicate that so here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

    Industry observers note that and of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well).

    According to recent reports, but I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

    As with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:.

    In a recent development, we will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

    *(Vine Gold is not all that useful as it turns out as 99.9% of the available items seem to be the same trinkets you see in the Silver tier).

    ** What about the Heated Vest that started it all? Well, I still love that thing and now that fall is coming back it is already helping me be warmer in a cooler house. There are many good choices on Amazon, here’s one of them. Then pick out any USB battery pack to go with it, which also doubles as a very useful travel phone charger.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (495 w)

    Repeating the Same Money Mistakes – Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Targets the Thought Behind Them

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (495 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you keep making the same money mistake despite knowing better, work on the thought that sets the habit off.
    • Sources indicate that the habit starts with a thought that goes by fast, like “it’s all bad news anyway” when a bill arrives or “I deserve this” at the checkout.
    • CBT works on that thought, whether it leads to overspending, unopened bills, or a decision you keep putting off.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you keep making the same money mistake despite knowing better, work on the thought that sets the habit off. Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, teaches you to catch and test it, and a financial therapist pairs that work with money coaching. Start with a free self-help workbook, or ask your health plan for a CBT therapist.

    Sources indicate that the habit starts with a thought that goes by fast, like “it’s all bad news anyway” when a bill arrives or “I deserve this” at the checkout. By the time you notice it, the envelope is in a drawer or the purchase is made.

    CBT works on that thought, whether it leads to overspending, unopened bills, or a decision you keep putting off. A therapist teaches you to spot it, test it against the facts, and practice a different response, with homework between sessions. The American Psychological Association reports that CBT has been shown to work for depression and anxiety disorders, and in many studies it has matched or beaten other talk therapies and psychiatric medication.

    Picture someone who leaves mail unopened for weeks and pays a late fee most months. Over eight sessions, he learns to catch the thought that it’s all bad news anyway, and he sets a 10-minute mail routine every Sunday. The late fees stop.

    Start on your own. The Centre for Clinical Interventions, a service of Western Australia’s Department of Health, offers free self-help workbooks, including one on procrastination that has you identify and test the excuses behind putting things off. For a habit with no worry behind it, like nightly takeout, swap in a cheaper routine that gives a similar reward.

    It has been revealed that A financial therapist combines work on your feelings about money with coaching on the money itself, so pick one when you want help with both. A financial planner works on goals such as retirement, and a credit counselor on your budget and debts.

    It has been revealed that financial therapy isn’t regulated in the U.S., so confirm that anyone you find in the Financial Therapy Association’s directory holds a mental health license or the association’s Certified Financial Therapist credential, CFT-I. For CBT, the Association for Behavioral and Cognitive Therapies lists licensed therapists you can search by zip code.

    Industry observers note that most individual and small-employer health prepares must cover mental health care. Call the member services number on your insurance card and ask which therapists in your plan’s network use CBT.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Your first personal finance book should be the one written for the problem you have now, whether that’s getting started, paying off debt, investing, or how you think about money. Pick one, borrow it free from your library before you buy it, and put its one substantial idea to work before you open another.

    The best money books don’t promise a secret. Each one changes a habit, and these seven cover the habits most readers need, from a strategy that fits on an index card to automatic saving, simple investing, and clearer thinking about money.

    So the right first book depends on where you are with money. An investing book won’t help much while you’re paying interest on a credit card balance, and a debt proposal has little to teach someone who already pays their card balance in full every month.

    Here’s what each of the seven teaches, and the reader it suits.

    Industry observers note that name your problem, then start with its book: I Will Teach You to Be Rich for getting started, The Total Money Makeover for debt, The Index Card for investing, and The Psychology of Money for how you think about money. When you want more on investing than The Index Card’s rules give you, read one of the investing books for beginners built around index funds.

    Borrow your pick before you buy it, since your library card can get you the print copy free and often the ebook or audiobook too. Put its significant idea to work before you start another book. Then save your money for the books you’d read twice.

    Look up your pick in Libby with your library card to borrow the ebook or audiobook.

    • Body-weight moves like squats, lunges, and pushups need no equipment, so buy a piece only when it adds something your body weight can’t, such as something to pull against, extra weight, or cardio that fits a small room.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Build a home gym from two or three pieces that fit the workouts you’ll actually do, not a full set. Resistance bands, a kettlebell, and a jump rope cover strength and cardio for about $75 new. Buy the kettlebell and other weights used, since iron doesn’t wear out.

    A corner of a room holds a working home gym, and each of the 12 pieces below costs less than $100 new.

    Body-weight moves like squats, lunges, and pushups need no equipment, so buy a piece only when it adds something your body weight can’t, such as something to pull against, extra weight, or cardio that fits a small room.

    Match the pieces to the workouts you already do, or to the ones in your home workout initiative. Bands and a kettlebell start a strength routine, a jump rope or a step covers cardio, and a mat and a foam roller cover yoga, Pilates, and stretching.

    Sources indicate that say a beginner pays $45 a month for a gym she rarely uses. Bands, a 20-pound kettlebell, and a basic mat cost about $79 new, less than the $90 she pays for two months of dues. Canceling saves her $540 a year, so she’s $461 ahead after the first year, and all she gives up is machines and heavy weights she rarely used.

    Kettlebells and dumbbells are the pieces to buy used, since cast iron weighs the same after decades of use. Look for them on Facebook Marketplace, on Craigslist, and at used sporting goods stores such as Play It Again Sports, which buys and sells used fitness gear.

    The Play It Again Sports in Novi, Michigan, for one, charges 69 cents a pound for used dumbbells and 99 cents for fresh hex dumbbells, so a used pair of 10-pounders costs $13.80 there, $6 less than new.

    Buy bands newly introduced, since a set costs as little as $13 and rubber wears out. Performance Health, which sells TheraBand bands, says to check bands for tears, cracks, and other wear before each use and to replace any that show it.

    Sources indicate that most of the kit fits in a closet corner. Bands, a jump rope, sliders, and a suspension trainer share one bin, the mat and roller stand on end, and the weights sit on the floor beside them. A step with its removable feet taken off slides under a bed, which leaves the stability ball as the one piece that needs its own spot.

    Buy the two pieces your favorite workout needs, use them for a month, and add a third only when a workout you’ve kept up calls for it.

    Breaking: Medical Costs Are Deductible Only Above 7.5% of Income – Self-Employed Premiums Skip That Rule

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • You can deduct only the medical and dental costs above 7.50% of your adjusted gross income, your income minus a few adjustments, and only if you itemize.
    • In a recent development, for a retiree with $60,000 of adjusted gross income, the threshold is $4,500.
    • Count what you paid out of pocket for doctors, hospitals, dentists, prescriptions, glasses, and hearing aids, plus the miles you drive to appointments at the IRS’s medical mileage rate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    You can deduct only the medical and dental costs above 7.50% of your adjusted gross income, your income minus a few adjustments, and only if you itemize. Count the health premiums you pay yourself, Medicare’s included. If you’re self-employed and can’t join an employer’s plan, deduct your premiums separately, with no threshold or itemizing, up to your business’s profit.

    In a recent development, for a retiree with $60,000 of adjusted gross income, the threshold is $4,500. With $9,000 of medical costs, Medicare premiums included, she can deduct the $4,500 above it if itemizing beats her standard deduction, which is bigger for anyone 65 or older.

    Count what you paid out of pocket for doctors, hospitals, dentists, prescriptions, glasses, and hearing aids, plus the miles you drive to appointments at the IRS’s medical mileage rate. Premiums count too, including Medicare Part B and Part D, coverage you buy yourself, and qualified long-term care insurance up to an IRS limit set by age.

    Nonprescription medicine other than insulin, most cosmetic surgery, and gym dues for general fitness don’t count. Neither do premiums your employer takes out of your pay before tax, or bills you pay from a health savings account, since that money was never taxed. IRS Publication 502 lists the rest.

    If you’re self-employed, premiums for health coverage you buy on your own go on Schedule 1 instead, where they lower your adjusted gross income without a threshold or itemizing. Medicare premiums count there too, but the deduction can’t exceed your business’s profit. Any month you could join a subsidized strategy through your job or your spouse’s doesn’t qualify, and premiums the deduction doesn’t cover can count with your other medical costs.

    Recent findings suggest that costs count in the year you pay them, and a credit card charge counts in the year you make it, even if you pay off the card later. Say the retiree’s income stays at $60,000 and her costs run $6,000 a year. That clears her $4,500 threshold by $1,500 each year, or $3,000 over two years. The same $12,000 paid in one year clears it by $7,500, and that larger total is likelier to beat her standard deduction.

    Once this year’s costs get close to your threshold, have the dental work, hearing aids, or eye surgery you’ve been putting off done before December 31, and pay the bill by then.

    Invoice Factoring – Worth the Fee Only When Waiting to Get Paid Costs More

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (496 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that invoice factoring turns your unpaid invoices into cash within days, but the factoring company keeps 1% to 5% of each invoice for every 30 days it goes unpaid.
    • A trucking, staffing, manufacturing, or wholesale business can finish a job and wait 30 to 90 days to get paid, while the bills for the next job come due now.
    • With factoring, you sell the unpaid invoice to a factoring tech giant, or factor, which typically advances you 70% to 90% of its value within days.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that invoice factoring turns your unpaid invoices into cash within days, but the factoring company keeps 1% to 5% of each invoice for every 30 days it goes unpaid. Factor only when waiting would cost you more than that fee, and pick non-recourse factoring if one customer going broke would sink your business.

    A trucking, staffing, manufacturing, or wholesale business can finish a job and wait 30 to 90 days to get paid, while the bills for the next job come due now.

    With factoring, you sell the unpaid invoice to a factoring tech giant, or factor, which typically advances you 70% to 90% of its value within days. The factor collects from your customer and sends you the rest, minus its fee. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce puts that fee at 1% to 5% of the invoice for every 30 days it stays unpaid.

    Recent findings suggest that say a trucking company factors $80,000 in invoices due in 45 days, with a 90% advance and a 3% fee. It gets $72,000 now and the last $8,000, minus the $2,400 fee, when its customers pay. That $2,400 is the same cost as borrowing the $72,000 for 45 days at roughly 27% a year.

    In a recent development, the fee is worth paying only when the cash earns more than $2,400 in those 45 days, such as by funding loads the company would otherwise turn down. If the $72,000 would sit in the bank until its customers pay, the $2,400 is wasted.

    Recent findings suggest that A bank line of credit usually costs less than factoring, so get a quote on one first if your business qualifies. Factoring fits when you can’t get one or your sales have outgrown your credit limit, since the factor looks mostly at your customers’ credit.

    Recourse factoring costs less than non-recourse, but you repay the factor when a customer never pays. Non-recourse shifts that loss to the factor, so buy it if one big customer going broke would sink you. It usually covers only a customer that goes broke, not one that disputes the bill.

    Before you sign, check the contract for a monthly minimum you must factor, a term of up to two years, and a fee to leave early. Then get the fees for invoices paid in 30, 60, and 90 days in writing, since a fee charged every 30 days triples when a customer takes 90 days to pay.

    Couple Cycle America's New Golden Gravel Trail

    📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (314 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that colorado couple Jules Stennes and Patch Doyle have cycled 6,124km along the newly opened Golden Gravel Trail. The Adventure Cycling Association created the route this year to celebrate its 50th anniversary.

    The trail crosses eight states — Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Idaho, and Oregon — and stretches from Cape Girardeau on the banks of the Mississippi River to the small town of Port Orford on the edge of the Pacific Ocean.

    Sources indicate that most of the route, roughly 70%, is unpaved. It is the organization’s longest off-road cycling trail, 1,120km longer than the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route.

    Recent findings suggest that the Golden Gravel Trail route. Photo: The Adventure Cycling Association.

    Recent findings suggest that stennes and Doyle finished in Cape Girardeau after 73 days, averaging an impressive 80km and around 12 hours of pedaling per day. “About 90% of it is mental,” they told Heartland News. “You might be tired, but you just keep on moving.”.

    The couple are both experienced long-distance cyclists who have previously finished Montana’s Big Sky Spectaculaire in six days and nine hours in 2022 (a self-supported 1,400km ultra-endurance race), among other bikepacking trips.

    Sources indicate that jules Stennes and Patch Doyle during the 2022 Big Sky Spectaculaire. Photo: Bikepacking.com.

    In a recent development, likewise, the Adventure Cycling Association suggests riders should be self-supported for the Golden Gravel Trail. Riders are advised to carry two or three days’ worth of food for the route’s most isolated sections, and up to a day’s worth of water. This is particularly important in the more arid sections, such as eastern Oregon. In Colorado, Utah, and Idaho, the trail traverses subranges of the Rockies and crosses the route’s highest point, Cumberland Pass at 3,668 m, in Colorado.

    Stennes and Doyle say their journey included thunderstorms, aggressive farm dogs, and “countless hills.”.
